To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the IBD of IBP39 contains a winged-helical motif that is similar to that of the ETS family of eukaryotic transcription factors and that it binds the Inr sequence of the core promoter.
the Inr binding protein 39kDa (IBP 39) is the only protein that recognizes the Inr and that it directly recruits RNAPII to the Inr to initiate transcription in Trichomonas.
the Inr-binding protein IBP39 is composed of two domains, an N-terminal winged-helix domain (IBD), and a C-terminal domain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural and functional characterization of the core promoter recognition machinery of a primitive eukaryote.
the structural basis of the recognition and binding of the initiator element by IBP39 and the role of the C domain in the recruitment of RNAP II to the promoter.
the structural basis of core promoter recognition in a primitive eukaryote and the evolutionary history of the transcription machinery in eukaryotic cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IBD of IBP39 has a prokaryotic winged-helix fold and that IBP39 has evolved from an ancestral ETS-like protein that has been recruited for transcription initiation in T. vaginalis.
IBP39 recognizes the Inr and recruits RNAP II to the core promoter.

IBP39 is a primitive eukaryotic TFIIB, but this is a statement that is difficult to make without a more complete understanding of how RNAP II interacts with the TATA box, the DPE, and the C domain of IBP39, and how these interactions influence the selection of transcription start sites in T. vaginalis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IBP39 recognizes the Inr and recruits RNAP II to initiate transcription.
the IBD structure reveals a novel winged-helix fold that binds the Inr and that the C domain interacts with RNAP II to initiate transcription.
IBP39 is the first eukaryotic transcription factor that has been shown to directly recruit RNAP II to the promoter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TATA box is not required for transcription initiation in T. vaginalis and that the Inr is recognized by an ETS-family protein.
IBP39 represents a new family of eukaryotic transcription factors that are likely present in the common ancestor of the eukaryotes.
IBP39, a transcription factor that is conserved in eukaryotic evolution from T. vaginalis to humans, is structurally related to the prokaryotic ETS-family of transcription factors.
